signal: This is the operational pricing manual for creative services firms. Blair Enns delivers a complete, executable system moving from value theory through proposal architecture through negotiation tactics through mindset. Every chapter names a rule, framework, or procedure. SNIPED has direct application in almost every section: the Reset $1,500 floor, the 3-option proposal architecture, the value conversation, the anchor-high rule, and the psychological underpinnings of premium-buyer behavior all map directly onto existing OS doctrine.
doctrine:
PRICING CREATIVITY FULL DOCTRINE (Blair Enns, 2018)

--- THEORY FOUNDATION ---
1. SUBJECTIVE VALUE: Value is not inherent in work; it exists only in the buyer's mind. Labor theory of value (price = effort) is empirically wrong. The correct frame: value = expected outcome / price, with emotional/risk factors as magnifiers, not additives.
2. VALUE TRIAD: Macdivitt & Wilkinson: all value breaks into (a) cost reductions, (b) revenue gains, (c) emotional contributions (prestige, risk avoidance, peace of mind, personal gain). Emotional contributions are multipliers of economic value, not add-ons.
3. FAIRNESS IS SUBJECTIVE: Fairness is a feeling, not a number. Target: the double thank-you moment — both parties genuinely grateful. Better communication justifies higher prices; every price increase must be accompanied by communication.
4. PRODUCER vs. MARKETER SPECTRUM: Efficiency culture (producer) and innovation culture (marketer) cannot coexist. Producers are price-takers. Marketers are price-makers. Timesheet culture forces producer-efficiency thinking. AGI/FTE benchmark: respectable = $160k, excellent = $250k+. Gap between $200k and $250k is the efficiency ceiling; firms above it value-price.
5. THREE PRICING MODES: (a) Inputs/time-and-materials: firm bears no risk, lowest prices; (b) Outputs/deliverables: firm takes delivery risk, price certainty premium; (c) Value: price tied to client's desired future state — highest prices. Default must be value; inputs/outputs reserved for specific tactical situations.
6. CAPACITY MANAGEMENT: Optimal client roster = 10-12 ongoing clients. Pareto applies: top 3 clients drive most revenue. Airline-model segmentation (Baker): First Class 10%, Business 20%, Premium Economy 30%, Economy 30%, Priceline 10%. MLOE formula: firm's annual AGI target / 10. To double a $1m firm, go from 10 clients at $100k average to 10 clients at $200k average — not from 10 clients to 20.
7. VALUE CHAIN: Client → Value → Price → Cost → Solutions. Cost-based is the opposite. Never think about solutions until price is set.

--- SIX RULES ---
RULE 1 — PRICE THE CLIENT, NOT THE JOB: Value is contextual; the same work is worth 1,000x more to GM than to John Doe's dealership. Always price the client's situation, not the deliverable. Never publish specific prices on a customized services firm's site. Publish only MLOE or ranges for qualification purposes.
RULE 2 — OFFER OPTIONS: Never present a single-option proposal. Three options minimum. Options shift the client's question from 'Is this worth it?' to 'Which is best?' — a question the brain can actually answer. Williams-Sonoma breadmaker effect: adding a $429 model made the $279 model sell. Three beats two; four works as well; five+ risks paradox of choice. Decoys are legitimate: options not meant to sell but to make the target option look good.
RULE 3 — ANCHOR HIGH: Lead with the most expensive option in every conversation. Kahneman/Tversky: anchors affect final price even when the anchor is arbitrary. Anchored group estimated prices 38% higher than unanchored. The anchor is not there to be purchased — it is there to pull the middle option up. 'What would we charge if money were no object?' = anchor price. Anchor option purchased < 20% of the time = normal; > 20% = both anchor and middle are priced too low. When anchor gets purchased, celebrate.
RULE 4 — SAY A PRICE BEFORE YOU SHOW A PRICE: Always state pricing guidance verbally before delivering a written proposal. Rule of Money: those who don't talk about money don't make it. Early objections are friends; late objections are enemies. Applies to existing clients too — even on a routine reorder, call ahead to name the number before the document lands.
RULE 5 — MASTER THE VALUE CONVERSATION: Four-step framework: (1) Commit client to desired future state using the 3-year question: 'It's three years from today and we're having coffee. You're really happy. What happened?' (2) Determine metrics of success — quantify each want/need. (3) Agree on value of success — translate metrics to profit impact; 'math intuitively discounted for uncertainty.' (4) Offer pricing guidance — contribute the high end (Y), let client contribute the low end (X). Anchoring against guaranteed value: 'If I could guarantee all of this, would one-third of first-year profit be fair compensation?' Four sale conversations: probative → qualifying → value → closing. The Flip: moment client moves you from vendor to expert. Conditions needed: (a) expert-not-vendor status established, (b) desired future state uncovered, (c) senior decision makers present.
RULE 6 — LIMIT UNPAID PROPOSALS TO ONE PAGE: Three columns, three prices. The oral proposal is the proposal; the document is the prop. Paid proposals = those requiring discovery work first → sell a diagnostic as Phase 1. Diagnostic deliverables = findings + recommendations + one-page options. Never send proposals unattended ('treat them like young children'). Closing = facilitation, not persuasion. Order: options conversation → agreement in principle → contract → signed contract + deposit.

--- KEY TIPS (Proposals) ---
- HIGH ANCHOR OPTION: Ask 'what would we do/charge if money were no object?' Factor uncertainty discount back in from guaranteed-value anchor established in value conversation. Contingency/performance options are legitimate anchor choices but balance portfolio risk (investment portfolio metaphor — some high-risk, some low).
- LOW OPTION: Identify buyer type first: price buyer (The Flip never happens, always vendor), poker player (pretends price-sensitive, actually value buyer), value buyer. Low option = block of time, stripped of all other value forms (terms, senior access, reporting, price certainty). Forces poker players to reveal themselves. Price buyer selection = acceptable if profitable; poker player will gravitate to middle.
- MIDDLE OPTION — MAKE THE MARGIN HERE: Middle gets selected ~2x as often as other two combined. The Home Depot Option: Diagnostic (tell you what to do) / Help you do it (middle) / We do it all (anchor). High-value forms to add to middle: knowledge transfer, oversight/QC, access to principals, standards guides, reporting structures, reserved capacity.
- RETAINERS: Three benefits: predictable revenue, resource allocation, relationship depth. Three failure modes: one party always unhappy (wrong incentives), cost-based by default, pushes to productization. Two legitimate uses: (1) strategic guidance / open access retainer (10%+ discount for 12-month advance), (2) implementation capacity. Wrong method: take annual budget and divide by 12 mechanically.
- LEASE VS. SELL: Challenge own assumptions. Website = software = should be leased monthly. French designer licensing IP back to clients. 'Power by the Hour' jet engine model. Client who wouldn't pay $50k paid $108k at $3k/month.
- ALTERNATIVE MODELS: Pay-what-you-like (Executive Shine model, signals confidence). Satisfaction guarantees (Maister model). Tip clauses (Cialdini: plant reciprocity seed at time of agreement or opportunity is lost). Points-based = unnecessary complexity. Sprints = cost-based, but can be combined with fixed-price discovery and milestone incentives (Lax model).

--- NEGOTIATING ---
- SELL RISK REDUCTION: Premium = insurance. Both meanings of 'premium' are the same word. Drucker: 'All profit comes from risk.' Price options as risk tranches — client chooses how much risk to keep vs. transfer. Speak to risk openly in closing conversation.
- NUDGES (choice architecture): Anchoring, social proof ('most clients choose middle'), bandwagon, framing effect, loss aversion (diagnostic close = client already in relationship, harder to exit), sunk cost, certainty/Dunning-Kruger, scarcity, charm pricing ($19k instead of $20k on target option), confirmation bias (use client's bias-to-validate by being the one who challenges — expert move).
- NEVER DISCOUNT (but rules when acceptable): Don't discount to win new business — ever. First engagement must always be profitable. Discounts = favors for loyal clients only. Document all discounts on invoice as 'courtesy discount' to prevent new-price interpretation. Ask client to name the discount amount rather than guessing. 'Going free' gesture for best clients on special projects is legitimate.
- ALTERNATIVES TO PRICE CUTS: Offer payment terms (lease/finance). Strip value from lower option. Use guarantees to overcome risk objection (guarantee Phase 1 only). Trade longer commitment for lower price (rarely good; no real economies of scale in most creative firms). Walk away — not the end, often a pause that inverts power.
- REMOVE PRICING FROM FRONT LINES: Policy as lever ('It's our policy'). Policy beats preferences every time in negotiation. Centralize pricing to someone not emotionally invested in deal, client, or craft. Chief Value Officer / Value Council (Baker). Post-engagement pricing review process is mandatory.
- NEGOTIATE LIKE A PRO: Power formula: P = desirability/desire. Don't overinvest (sunk cost in time, emotion, money signals neediness). Stop negotiating when you've won — ask if you've already won before making concessions. Out-wait the waiter (procurement always lies — 'it's down to two firms' = almost certainly false). Decide give-gets in advance. Neuter final negotiators by pre-briefing the client on what procurement will do. Alternative forms of no: Positive No (reframe the need), 'How would I do that?' (Voss), 'Yes, but' (reveal trade-offs). Don't negotiate against yourself — Columbo pattern. Beware the Rabbit (used as price-lever; ask if you're the rabbit). Beware the White Knight (internal hero who gives away margin).

--- UNTETHERING FROM TIME ---
Transition path: (1) Apply new model to new clients only; (2) Value-price strategy first, then creative concepts, then initial application, leave re-application as commodity. Tracking time transition: (1) Free non-time-sellers from timesheets first; (2) Track firm-wide AGI/FTE instead of job-by-job. Time is a limiting mental construct — Dan Sullivan's two stages: hard work gets you to Stage 1; innovation + saying no gets you to Stage 2.

--- MINDSET ---
- Self-esteem is the largest determinant of gross profit. PP = M × A × SE.
- Baker: confidence comes from (a) deeply held beliefs and (b) options (new biz pipeline > capacity).
- Dysfunctional money ideas: hoarding, egalitarianism-as-fairness conflation, labor theory default under stress, scarcity mindset (zero-sum).
- Abundance framing: trade creates wealth; intangibles economy grows without resource extraction; Diamandis dematerialization argument.
supports: status/pricing: Full pricing system — the value-conversation framework, 3-option architecture, anchor-high mechanics, MLOE formula, buyer-type segmentation (price/poker/value), and the double-thank-you signal are all directly load-bearing for SNIPED's pricing decisions at every tier

positioning/sales-flow: The 4-conversation sale arc (probative/qualifying/value/closing), The Flip concept, vendor-vs-expert positioning, procurement tactics, and the Win Without Pitching alignment confirm SNIPED's anti-pitch, expert-practitioner lane

offer-design: 3-column proposal architecture, Home Depot option, diagnostic-as-Phase-1, retainer structuring, lease-vs-sell model, and the value chain (Client → Value → Price → Cost → Solutions) govern how SNIPED packages and sequences any Brand System or Op Kit offer

discovery/proof-loop: The 4-step value conversation (3-year question, metrics, value quantification, pricing guidance) is the operational script for SNIPED's discovery calls — especially the 'desired future state' framing and the anchoring-against-guaranteed-value technique

capital-allocation/money: MLOE formula, capacity management (10-12 client cap), AGI/FTE benchmarks ($160k floor, $250k+ value-pricer range), client portfolio as investment portfolio (risk balance), payment terms as competitive advantage, deposit policy

hospitality: The double thank-you framing maps directly to Guidara's hospitality doctrine — the goal is not extraction but mutual enrichment; satisfaction guarantees and tip clauses are service-hospitality expressions

leverage/possibility: Producer vs. marketer spectrum and the innovation-vs-efficiency trade-off directly support the leverage logic (code+media > labor). Saying no to create time for innovation = Naval's leverage principle operationalized
contradictions: OS Intel doc intel_pricing_logic.md references 3-option architecture and premium-as-insurance but does not surface the specific buyer-type taxonomy (price buyer / poker player / value buyer) — this is a meaningful gap; the poker-player frame changes how SNIPED should respond to early fee pushback from founder prospects who may be bluffing

OS retail floor of $1,500 (Reset price) is below the book's recommended MLOE for even a $15k-per-year firm ($1,500); the Reset is appropriately positioned as a trial/entry point but should be explicitly framed as below-MLOE capacity access to signal it is the exception, not the standard — otherwise it risks training buyers that SNIPED is a price-taker

The book explicitly warns against all-retainer models and the productization trap — OS has explored retainer structures for social/content work; these should be scoped only as the two legitimate retainer forms (strategic open-access OR implementation-capacity), not as default monthly agreements

Book says never give free advice in the sale (no free diagnostic, no free strategic recommendations in proposals) — OS currently produces extensive free content (Direction Stack, cultural docs); Enns would frame this as 'thought leadership as probative conversation' which is legitimate, but any direct pre-proposal diagnostic work for a prospect should be framed as a paid diagnostic

Book states pricing strategy should come before solutions — the OS workflow sometimes moves to deliverable scoping (shoot planning, composite planning) before pricing is set; this is the cost-based sequence Enns explicitly identifies as the primary pricing failure mode
chunk_accuracy_note: The 12 existing chunks capture the theoretical foundations and a handful of structural rules accurately (subjective value, 3-option proposal, anchor-high, double thank-you, walk-away, productize-not-itemize). However they substantially miss or distort the following: (1) The 4-step value conversation framework — the most operationally important content in the book — has no dedicated chunk; the 'Permission Conversation' chunk is an invention not found in the text (Enns uses no such named technique; the actual technique is the 3-year question and the 4-step framework); (2) Buyer-type segmentation (price buyer / poker player / value buyer) is absent; (3) The full negotiation toolkit (remove from front lines, policy invocation, out-wait, neuter procurement, positive no, how-would-I-do-that) is entirely absent; (4) The retainer analysis (when retainers fail, two proper uses) is absent; (5) The producer/marketer spectrum and AGI/FTE benchmarks are absent; (6) The lease-vs-sell chapter is absent; (7) The mindset chapter (self-esteem as PP multiplier, scarcity vs. abundance) is absent. The 'get paid before you do the work' chunk overstates a specific 50% deposit rule — the book's deposit advice is more situational. The deposit chunk conflates the book's terms chapter with a rule Enns does not state that bluntly.
skill_candidates: value-conversation-script: 4-step executable framework — commit desired future state / set metrics / agree value / offer pricing guidance — run as a pre-proposal ritual before any Brand System or Op Kit quote is drafted

3-option-proposal-builder: Given a client context and a desired outcome, generate three options (low=time-block, middle=Home Depot/high-margin, anchor=money-no-object) with risk framing for the closing conversation
gate_candidates: pricing-sequence-gate: Before any proposal is drafted, confirm value conversation was conducted and price was arrived at BEFORE solutions were designed — if solutions came first, restart with value chain (Client → Value → Price → Cost → Solutions)
buyer-type-gate: Before any negotiation concession, identify buyer type (price / poker / value); never cut price for a poker player without first presenting the stripped low option
workflow_candidates: post-engagement-pricing-review: After every closed engagement, run the retrospective question — 'knowing what we know now, how would we reprice?' — and update the pricing reference doc; maps to Enns's recommendation of a standardized post-engagement review
